## **The Sound of Inventory**

The first time I learned what a warehouse smells like, I mistook it for rain.

Not the clean, metallic rain that falls in films and settles in gutters with a kind of cinematic purity. I mean the rain that gets dragged in by shoes and then forgotten, the damp that seeps into concrete and lingers until it becomes part of the building’s weather. The warehouse where I worked was a long, low structure with fluorescent lights that never quite decided whether they were on. The air was cool in the way hospitals are cool—intentionally, clinically, as if discomfort were something the company could bill for. Every few feet, a pallet jack leaned against the edge of a world that had no corners, only aisles.

I wasn’t there to build anything. I was there to count.

Inventory is a quiet religion. People like to imagine warehouses as engines of speed—forklifts, beeps, motion everywhere. That’s true on the surface. Underneath, it is a place of stillness punctuated by small, repeated motions: scan, confirm; scan, confirm; pick, place; scan, confirm. The machines have their own steady language, and the human mind, if it’s willing, will learn to speak it with its own pauses.

When you count the same item enough times, you start to recognize the personality of mistakes. Some errors are cheerful, almost accidental: a label stuck to a neighboring box, a barcode smudged in a way that makes the scanner hesitate like a person pretending they didn’t hear you. Other mistakes are stubborn and deliberate, the kind made by a system that wasn’t designed for reality. A bin is supposed to contain three cases. It contains three cases plus a fourth that someone must have moved in a hurry, or maybe last year, or maybe as a punishment.

At first I assumed the warehouse was a place where randomness was eliminated. But the longer I stayed, the more I realized that randomness isn’t eliminated; it just gets categorized. In a well-run warehouse, randomness gets translated into spreadsheets.

There were two spreadsheets I came to know as intimately as I knew my own handwriting.

The first was called something like *Cycle Count Variance*. It was mostly numbers and arrows, and it told me, in an impersonal way, what the system expected to be true and what had refused to cooperate. The second was the one that felt alive: *Damaged/Disposed*. It was full of brief notes, a few words each, the bureaucratic equivalents of shrugging. “Crushed corner.” “Moisture exposure.” “Box torn.”

The items were not poetry, but people treated them as if they were. When something was “crushed corner,” you could almost see the conveyor belt nudging it like a careless elbow. When something was “moisture exposure,” the note carried a faint accusation: not weather, but negligence; not happenstance, but a chain of choices.

I didn’t think about negligence much at the beginning. I thought about speed. Speed meant less overtime. Less overtime meant I could go home before the night got heavy. The warehouse was a place where time was measured in productivity and the clock did its best impression of a judge.

Then, on a Tuesday that would have been like any other Tuesday if the world had kept its promises, the scanner refused.

It wasn’t the dramatic kind of refusal where an alarm blares and everyone scrambles. It was more subtle. The screen displayed a message that might as well have been a sigh: *Item not found.*

I stared at it, thumb hovering over the confirm button. The pallet was right there—sturdy, wrapped in film, labeled with the company’s clean fonts that looked as if they were designed by a committee afraid of mistakes. I checked the label again. Same SKU. Same numbers.

My coworker—his name was Marco, though everyone just said “Marco” like it was a verb—came over with the relaxed confidence of someone who’d seen the warehouse disagree before. He took one look and said, “Probably a ghost.”

“A ghost?”

“Yeah. Something got moved without the system knowing.”

“That doesn’t happen,” I said, because the mind likes certainty. The mind likes to believe that if the computer says something, it must be right. Or, at least, that the computer is right until proven otherwise by evidence.

Marco shrugged. “It happens all the time.”

We did what you do when something doesn’t make sense: we tried again. We scanned the barcode from another angle, like we were asking for forgiveness from a shy oracle. We adjusted the scanner. We verified that the label matched the system’s location. We checked the adjacent bins.

The pallet didn’t belong there.

Or rather, it belonged there in the way a stranger’s coat can belong on your chair: physically present, emotionally misplaced, waiting for someone to notice. The system insisted the bin should be empty. The warehouse insisted it wasn’t.

When you work inventory, you become familiar with a certain kind of paranoia. It doesn’t feel like paranoia. It feels like being responsible. If something is missing, someone has to explain why. If something is in the wrong place, someone has to account for it. The warehouse doesn’t create stories; it forces you to become a storyteller against your will.

Marco walked away after we couldn’t make it behave. He left me with the kind of unresolved question that, in another life, might have become a mystery novel. Here, it became a task. I had to decide what to do with the pallet: move it to the correct location, hold it in quarantine, or create a note in the system so the system would remember it later.

I chose the least dramatic option: I moved it.

It felt like stealing, at first—taking something from the universe where it had mistakenly ended up and returning it to the place the universe had planned. When the pallet jack rolled under the weight, it made that familiar groaning sound that always seemed to rise from the floor rather than from the wheels. The warehouse swallowed the sound and gave it back as silence.

When I scanned the barcode at the new bin, the system finally agreed. *Item found.* The green letters appeared like approval.

I should have been relieved. Instead I felt uneasy. Because the system’s agreement didn’t prove anything about the pallet. It proved only that the system’s expectations could be matched by manipulation. That’s what software is, in the end: a set of expectations that can be satisfied, sometimes honestly and sometimes through the kind of careful rearranging that looks like honesty from far away.

Later, during the break where the warehouse’s air-conditioning seemed to relax just enough for humans to remember they were animals, I looked up the SKU.

The item was unremarkable: a case pack of something meant for consumption and use—something that would end up in a store, on a shelf, inside a home where people would use it without thinking about the chain that brought it there. The SKU corresponded to a brand name I couldn’t recall later, and a product photo I couldn’t interpret. In the warehouse, objects existed in categories. Outside the warehouse, they existed in lives.

That night, after I drove home through streets that smelled like summer and exhaust, I couldn’t stop thinking about the pallet.

How did it arrive in the wrong bin? Why hadn’t someone caught it? Was it damaged? Had it been moved once already, and someone had decided the system was optional?

I tried to shake the thoughts off by doing normal things: eating, washing dishes, letting the day dissolve. But inventory had a way of making the world feel like it had a ledger. Everything began to look like it could be counted. Every emotion began to feel like it had a category.

The next day I came in and ran the cycle count for that aisle again. Not because I was told to, but because I couldn’t stand leaving the mistake unexamined. Sometimes mistakes are evidence. Sometimes they are just noise.

I checked the bin where the pallet had originally been—where the system had insisted there should be emptiness.

There was now emptiness.

But the system still showed a variance number from the previous count. A number that meant, at some earlier point in time, the bin had contained something it shouldn’t have. Maybe my pallet had been that something. Maybe someone else’s pallet, already moved or disposed.

In the inventory world, time isn’t measured in days the way humans measure it. It’s measured in counts. Every count is a snapshot of a system’s belief. The variance numbers were footprints left by disbelief.

I pulled the *Cycle Count Variance* report for that bin. It contained a history of attempts to reconcile reality with expectation. It showed small discrepancies—sometimes overcounting, sometimes undercounting—always corrected eventually, always accompanied by the same kind of sterile notes: “Adjusted.” “Reviewed.” “Verified.”

No explanation, not really. No story. Just the system cleaning up after itself.

But there was one line item that didn’t match the pattern.

The note attached to that variance record included a phrase I hadn’t seen before: “Moved to dead location.”

Dead location.

In the language of the warehouse, “dead location” meant a place where items were stored temporarily before they were either corrected or disposed of. It was a bin that didn’t participate in the neat fiction of inventory accuracy. It was a holding cell for objects that didn’t know what they were supposed to be. A place for confusion.

And the note had a date that didn’t align with any of the other counts. It had been recorded two weeks earlier, after the previous discrepancy should have been resolved.

I sat there, staring at the report, feeling the way you feel when you realize a story’s timeline has been subtly rearranged.

When you work inventory long enough, you start to recognize the rhythm of human error. It usually follows a predictable pattern: a hurried scan, a label misread, a box shoved into the wrong bin because someone was thinking about something else. Those errors are like dropped objects—accidents with physical momentum.

But “dead location” sounded like intention. It sounded like a choice to hide the truth in a place where nobody would look too closely.

I decided I would ask someone.

Marco was the first person I saw who seemed like he might answer without sounding alarmed. I approached him during the lull between forklift waves.

“Hey,” I said, trying to make my voice casual. “Do you know what ‘dead location’ means?”

Marco’s eyes flicked to mine like a quick check for sincerity. Then he looked away, toward the aisles where pallets sat in orderly ranks like books on shelves.

“It’s where they put stuff if it’s—” He paused, searching for neutral language. “If it’s not supposed to be on the regular floor.”

“Not supposed to be?”

“Sometimes, things come in damaged. Sometimes they get mislabeled. They want it out of the system until it’s sorted.”

“That’s… fine,” I said, though it didn’t feel fine.

Marco sighed. “Look. You’re new-ish. You’ll learn. Everyone thinks they’re doing the right thing.”

His tone was careful. He didn’t mean it as advice. He meant it as a warning: a hint that the truth here wasn’t a simple line from cause to effect. It was a web of motivations.

“You think something’s been hidden?” I asked.

Marco gave me a look that wasn’t exactly pity, but it wasn’t not-pity.

“I think,” he said slowly, “that the system doesn’t like admitting uncertainty. So people try to make uncertainty smaller.”

That was the closest he came to an explanation. But it left me with something worse than an answer: it left me with a principle.

Make uncertainty smaller.

In the warehouse, uncertainty was not just a technical problem. It was a moral hazard. It meant work. It meant people asking questions. It meant possibly getting in trouble for not following procedure. So if uncertainty could be contained in a dead location, it could be postponed. And postponement, in many systems, is a kind of forgiveness.

I returned to my scanner and kept counting.

The day passed like days do when you stop trusting your own mind: you move through tasks, you scan barcodes, you confirm labels, and you pretend your thoughts are just background noise. But later, when I looked at my log for the day, I noticed something that made my hands go cold.

The SKU for that pallet—now correctly located—was scheduled for removal the next day.

Removal.

Not because of damage. Not because of a recall. Because the system showed it would be “returned” to a supplier or “disposed” for reasons unknown. The product had an action assigned, the kind of action that usually happens when an order changes or a contract ends. But this schedule didn’t match the pattern of similar SKUs.

It wasn’t removal in response to demand. It was removal in response to something earlier and unseen.

In other words, the warehouse might have intended to erase the pallet from its records not because it needed to, but because it wanted to.

That thought made me uncomfortable in a way that wasn’t just fear. It felt like being asked to participate in a cover-up you don’t know how to refuse.

I didn’t have power here. I had a scanner and a job title that meant I was trusted to count, not to judge. My role was to report numbers, not to interpret motives. Still, the human mind doesn’t stay silent when faced with patterns that feel like stories.

I went home that night and couldn’t sleep. I thought about the dead location. I thought about how the inventory system would eventually update itself, correcting the counts, making the mistake disappear from variance reports. The system would eventually forget the pallet had ever been in the wrong bin. Forgetting is the most efficient form of erasure.

In the dark, I remembered a childhood habit: when I was asked to clean my room, I would move objects from one pile to another instead of throwing anything away. My parents would look at the visible surface and believe I had tidied. I became a specialist in appearance.

I realized that warehouses build their own childhood rooms. Not through malice, but through habit. People learn to make things look correct. The numbers get satisfied. The shelves look orderly. The company can sleep.

But what if what we call accuracy is just a performance?

What if the system can be “correct” while reality continues to rot underneath?

Those thoughts could have gone nowhere, turning into the kind of anxious spirals people have when their job becomes too heavy. But then, two nights later, a coworker I didn’t know very well stopped me near the break room.

He said, “Are you the one who moved that pallet?”

I felt my stomach drop. I hadn’t told anyone I moved it, not outside of the basic trace in the system log. But perhaps the warehouse was not as secretive as I assumed. Perhaps the pallet had become a small rumor, a thing people watched because it didn’t belong.

“Yes,” I said carefully.

“Why’d you do that?”

I could have answered with the official explanation: to align with system location, to correct misplacement, to ensure accuracy. But those phrases sounded like excuses even as I spoke them. So I told the truer version: “Because it didn’t match the bin, and it bothered me.”

He didn’t smile. He didn’t scold. He nodded once, like someone acknowledging another person has the same kind of trouble.

“They’re going to get rid of it,” he said.

“Already?”

He shrugged. “Soon. Maybe tomorrow. That’s what I heard.”

“Do you know why?”

“Not officially,” he said. “But—” He hesitated. His eyes darted to the warehouse floor through the glass doors. “Sometimes they move things into dead locations because they don’t want to deal with returns. Or because a customer will complain if the wrong batch ships.”

“Wrong batch?”

He looked uncomfortable again, as if the words were sticky. “Look. I can’t say more.”

And then he left me there with the kind of uncertainty that feels like a key turning in a lock. It didn’t create a clear plot. It created a new kind of dread: the sense that there was a reason the system was being manipulated, and that the reason involved someone else’s time, someone else’s trust, someone else’s life.

If inventory errors were only mistakes, they could be forgiven. But if they were part of a pattern—if dead locations were a strategy—then the moral question becomes larger than one pallet. It becomes a question about what we allow to be true when the world is run by systems that optimize for convenience.

The next day, the pallet was gone.

Not just physically gone, but functionally gone. The bin showed empty. The system updated its records. The variance report no longer showed the earlier discrepancy. The spreadsheet was scrubbed clean.

The warehouse could breathe again.

But I couldn’t. Not really.

In the weeks that followed, I kept working. The job didn’t change. The scanner kept beeping. The pallets kept arriving in their plastic cocoons. Time kept going.

Yet something in me had shifted. I began to notice patterns I used to ignore.

A certain kind of damage label appeared more often on shipments that were never fully investigated. Certain SKUs seemed to vanish more quickly after certain dates. When I asked a supervisor about one discrepancy, the response was always the same: “It’s been adjusted.”

Adjusted. Adjusted. Adjusted.

As if human lives were adjustable in the same way numbers are.

One afternoon I overheard a manager speaking on the radio with a supplier. Their voices were calm, professional, as if they were negotiating the weather. But I caught phrases like “dead stock,” “temporary hold,” and “no paperwork on this end.” There was laughter too, soft and quick, like a joke told by someone who assumed consequences were not real.

I turned away. My body moved with the reflex of someone who doesn’t want to become a problem.

But later, in the quiet aisle where I scanned barcodes, I thought about what inventories are for.

We inventory what matters. We count what we can sell. We track what people will use. We measure, categorize, and store because we want continuity: the belief that what we have will be what we need later.

Yet the warehouse revealed a different truth: continuity can be fabricated. Belief can be engineered. If enough people agree that the system’s version of reality is the only reality that matters, then the rest becomes invisible. The warehouse becomes a place where the invisible is not just hidden—it is treated as nonexistent.

I started to wonder whether the “inventory” we were keeping was not the product but the story.

The story of care.

The story that our company is competent.

The story that mistakes are rare and accidents are isolated.

I started to feel like my job was not to protect the truth, but to protect the appearance of truth. Counting made me useful. But counting also made me complicit, because my adjustments helped the system continue to look credible.

In some ways, it was a classic human trap: the moment you participate in something, you become part of its momentum.

One evening, nearing the end of my shift, I was assigned to scan a pallet destined for disposal. The pallet was wrapped and labeled, the way all disposal items were wrapped, as if nothing could be allowed to touch the rest of the warehouse’s cleanliness. There was a note on the label: *Condition: questionable.*

Questionable. It sounded polite. It sounded like the product had offended someone’s standards without fully breaking them.

I scanned it. The system accepted.

I began to think about my earlier pallet—the one that had gone into the wrong bin, then moved, then removed. The question I couldn’t escape was simple and corrosive: how often had I scanned things into existence that were already doomed?

Maybe the dead location wasn’t just a holding cell. Maybe it was a way to decide what stories would survive. Maybe “dead stock” wasn’t about inventory—it was about narrative control. It was a place where problematic truths could wait until they were convenient to ignore.

I looked at the plastic wrap. Under it, the product shifted slightly as the pallet settled on the floor. It didn’t look monstrous. It didn’t look like fraud. It looked like goods—objects, materials, nothing but the raw stuff of commerce.

But then I thought about the people who would consume these goods, the people who trusted that the warehouse system was a map rather than a mask. I imagined a customer opening a box and finding damage that had been covered up, or a batch that didn’t match the labeling. I imagined someone complaining, someone filling out paperwork, someone becoming angry and powerless. I imagined a ripple of frustration caused by small, repeated decisions to hide uncertainty.

Maybe that was the most human part of the story: the way small choices accumulate until they become a machine of harm.

The next morning, I called the hotline.

I didn’t do it with bravado. I did it while sitting in my car in a parking lot, hands trembling slightly on the steering wheel. The hotline was meant for reporting fraud or safety violations. I had no proof of wrongdoing in the legal sense—only patterns, notes, phrases like “no paperwork,” and the uncomfortable feeling that my scanner had been used as a tool to clean up evidence.

I told the hotline representative as much as I could without sounding like I was inventing a thriller. I described the dead location note. I mentioned the variance report. I explained how certain pallets were moved and then removed soon after without clear reason. I described the timing mismatches. I described overheard phrases, carefully, as “what I heard,” not as “what I know.”

After I hung up, I waited for guilt to vanish. Instead, guilt grew. Because once you report something, you can’t pretend you’re neutral anymore. You become a person with a side, even if you didn’t choose to have one.

But I also felt something else: relief. A small, fragile relief that came from refusing to let the warehouse’s story erase your own.

I returned to work. Nobody accused me. Nobody threatened me. The day continued in its usual beeping rhythms. But when I scanned items, I began to notice the way coworkers spoke more quietly. I noticed how questions were avoided. I noticed how a supervisor’s tone changed when I asked for clarification.

The system didn’t collapse. It didn’t explode into confession. Bureaucracies don’t work that way. Instead, the system did what systems do: it adapted. It tightened. It made new procedures and called them improvements.

Some pallets were held longer. Some notes got reviewed. Some dead locations were emptied with more urgency.

In other words, the story shifted slightly.

Not enough to satisfy my hope, not enough to make me feel heroic. But enough to suggest that my small action had nudged the machine away from its old habits.

The warehouse remained a warehouse. It still smelled like damp concrete and fluorescent light. The aisles still stretched like corridors in a dream you can’t wake from. The scanner still beeped with patient indifference.

Yet in the middle of all that, I learned something I hadn’t expected when I started counting boxes.

Inventory teaches you that accuracy is not a single act. It is a system of continuous choices: where you place things, how you record them, what you allow to count as “close enough,” what you dismiss as negligible, what you refuse to see because you’ve trained yourself not to.

The truth is fragile. It can be lost not because it is hidden by evil villains, but because people are busy and tired and prefer the clean story. Truth gets worn away by repetition. Truth gets replaced by compliance.

But truth can also be rebuilt, not by one dramatic moment, but by a thousand small refusals to let uncertainty disappear into dead locations.

Sometimes those refusals look like nothing. They look like a person asking a question instead of accepting an “adjusted.” They look like scanning from a different angle instead of shrugging. They look like making a note in a system and insisting that the system remember.

Sometimes they look like a phone call in a quiet car.

And sometimes they look like the simple decision to be honest in the middle of a place designed for approximation.

I don’t know what happened to that first pallet after it was removed. I like to believe it was disposed responsibly, that it had been genuinely damaged, that the confusion was an accident. I like to believe people can be better than their systems.

But I also know that belief is not evidence. In warehouses—and in lives—evidence is what remains when the stories stop flattering us.

The last day I worked there, I stood at the end of an aisle and watched a forklift roll past like a slow animal. The pallets were stacked higher than my chest, wrapped in plastic that caught the light like skin. Workers moved with practiced efficiency, scanning, confirming, adjusting.

I tried to listen for the sound of inventory.

It isn’t just beeps. It isn’t just the hiss of pallet film tearing. It isn’t even the quiet groan of wheels.

The sound of inventory is the sound of a system asking the world to agree with it. It is the sound of people trying to live inside that agreement. It is the sound of small corrections, repeated until they become truth by habit.

And underneath it all, if you pay attention, there’s another sound: the soft resistance of reality.

Reality doesn’t shout. It doesn’t announce itself with alarms. It simply refuses to fit perfectly into bins.

If you’re lucky—if you’ve learned how to count without forgetting—you notice the refusal.

Then you decide what kind of person you’re going to be when the warehouse asks you to do something convenient instead of something true.

---

If you want, I can tailor the style next time (more fiction, more essay, darker, funnier, more lyrical, etc.) or write a different ~2500-word piece on a topic you choose.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first time I noticed the quiet cruelty of morning, I was standing in a place I didn’t choose.

It wasn’t that the sidewalk was hostile. It wasn’t even cold in a dramatic way, the kind of cold that makes you feel like a hero in a movie. It was just early—too early for conversation, too early for decisions, too early for the mind to finish waking up. The air had that thin, washed quality that makes everything look slightly unfinished. Streetlights still hung around as if they had forgotten their cue, and the buildings—those dependable blocks of brick and glass—seemed to hold their breath.

I was waiting for a bus, though “waiting” is a polite word. I was more like pinned in place by habit, an insect immobilized by the soft insistence of routine. My phone was in my pocket. I had no intention of taking it out. It wasn’t guilt or bravery; it was simply the vague hope that if I didn’t look, I wouldn’t have to be reminded that time moves even when you’re not ready for it.

A woman walked past me carrying a paper bag with two handles that kept twisting in her grip. She moved like someone who knew exactly where she was going, and I resented her competence for the briefest possible moment, the way you might resent a person whose umbrella doesn’t turn inside out. Then she was gone, leaving behind only the faint smell of coffee and something fried.

The bus arrived with a sigh of brakes, and the door opened like a reluctant confession. I stepped inside and slid into a seat that faced forward, as if looking ahead might make the day behave. The driver didn’t greet anyone. He didn’t scowl. He just sat there with his hands at rest, the way certain people do when they’ve learned that emotion is optional at certain hours.

Outside the window, the city unfolded in slices: street after street, block after block, all of them equally awake and equally indifferent. In my head, my thoughts performed that familiar balancing act—half philosophical, half practical. Why do we call this “a day” when it begins without permission? Why do we act surprised when the hours pass? Why do we pretend there’s a clean line between the life we want and the life we have?

The bus rocked and my mind began to drift into those thin, unguarded memories that come like stray cats: you don’t invite them, but you feed them anyway. I remembered an argument from years ago. Not because it was significant in any objective way, but because it was still unfinished inside me. A sentence I had swallowed. A question I hadn’t asked. The version of myself I could have been if I’d chosen courage over caution.

When I reached my stop, I stood with everyone else, a choreography of bodies that didn’t require individual thought. The doors opened. Cold air entered like a ghost. I stepped out onto the sidewalk and felt, briefly, that small shock of being transferred back into the world.

My day, like most days, did not begin with fireworks. It began with a list.

I had told myself I would be better. Better at planning. Better at following through. Better at not letting the day become a series of accidents. I wrote my tasks in a notebook as if ink had the power to bind the future to my will. In the margins I made small marks—tiny stars, circles, checkmarks—symbols that looked like progress but were mostly a way of negotiating with uncertainty.

At the first appointment, I sat in a room that smelled faintly of disinfectant and old magazines. The magazines were new enough to seem current but worn enough to suggest they’d been read by too many people who were waiting for too many things. The receptionist smiled with the practiced warmth of someone who understands that smiles don’t fix problems, but they can soften the edges.

When my name was called, I stood and followed a hallway that seemed longer than it should have been. The door opened into a space where the air changed—warmer, less stale. A professional greeted me with a voice engineered for calm.

We talked. We recorded facts. We discussed options, which is a polite phrase for admitting that none of the choices are clean. The conversation was efficient, almost merciful in its clarity. But as I spoke, I realized something: I wasn’t only trying to solve a problem. I was trying to explain myself.

There is a specific kind of loneliness in explaining yourself to a stranger. You don’t want sympathy, but you want understanding. You want your inner life to be seen without being consumed. You want to be translated accurately, without distortion. The worst part is that you can feel yourself performing—the way you choose details and omit others, the way your voice becomes slightly more organized when you think it’s being evaluated.

When the appointment ended, I thanked the professional and walked out. Outside, the sky had brightened but not softened. The light was hard, as if the sun were trying to prove something.

I checked my notebook again. The list looked smaller now, which should have felt satisfying. Instead it made me anxious. Completed items are supposed to be relief, but for me they became evidence that time could move too quickly. The future is always hungry, waiting for the present to finish.

On the bus home—or rather, on the bus between tasks—I watched people in the way you might watch weather. Not to judge it, exactly, but to recognize patterns. The teenage boy with headphones and a posture that suggested he was listening to music and also bracing against something he wouldn’t name. The man with a laptop open, typing carefully like he was writing on fragile glass. The woman who kept checking her wrist even though there was no watch there.

Everyone had a story going on inside them. Most of those stories were private. But all of them moved with the same invisible current.

At a stop near a park, the bus paused long enough for me to hear laughter. It wasn’t loud, but it had a clean shape. Someone—children or a group of young adults—laughed the way you laugh when you feel safe enough to take up space.

I wanted to be jealous. That would be easy. But instead I felt something stranger: the tenderness of recognition. I remembered what it felt like to be laughed at without fear, to be witnessed without judgment. I remembered that my body used to believe in tomorrow.

I got off the bus and walked toward the park. The path curved, and as it did, I noticed little things I usually ignored: a tree with a split trunk, new growth sprouting from the side like a stubborn idea; a poster on a pole advertising an event that might have nothing to do with me but was still proof that people were planning; a stray dog curled asleep under a bench as if the world were gentle enough to allow it.

The park was not the sanctuary I had imagined, not a place untouched by life. It was full of everyday friction: joggers passing too close, couples speaking in low voices that sometimes rose too quickly. People were doing what people do when they’re trying to fill their time with meaning.

I sat on a bench and watched the shadows shift. At some point, I realized that the day was not asking me for anything dramatic. It wasn’t demanding that I solve my biggest problem or become the person I had been promising myself. It was simply continuing, offering me small opportunities to notice.

There’s a myth that growth is loud: the big change, the breakthrough, the dramatic decision. But I have experienced growth more often as a quiet adjustment—like learning to walk a step differently after an injury. You don’t announce it. You just find that you’re less careful or more steady. You realize, in hindsight, that something inside you has healed enough to let you move on.

While I sat there, my mind tried to sprint ahead. It started listing all the ways I could fail. It started imagining conversations I didn’t want. It started rehearsing disasters the way some people rehearse speeches.

I’ve learned that the mind often mistakes repetition for preparation. It thinks if it runs the same scenario enough times, it will be ready when it happens. But the problem is that it doesn’t run in the direction of wisdom. It runs in circles, and the loop becomes a kind of prison.

So I did something small. I didn’t “fix my life.” I didn’t banish anxiety through sheer willpower. I just brought my attention back to the present: the feeling of sun on my hands, the sound of wind in leaves, the distant squeak of a bicycle chain. I listened for the way those sensations changed over a minute. My mind complained the whole time, but it gradually loosened, as if irritated by having to stay grounded.

It’s embarrassing, this need to return again and again. I used to think that being anxious meant I cared too much. Now I think it often means I’m stuck in a story that pretends it’s protecting me.

A child ran past me chasing a ball that bounced with bright insistence. The ball rolled under the bench, and the child crouched to retrieve it. For a moment, the child’s face was close enough to see the texture of their expression—the concentration, the brief frustration, the immediate triumph. The child didn’t apologize for being in the way. They didn’t worry about whether the world would approve of their movements. Their joy was allowed to be messy.

I wondered what happens to people when joy becomes something they have to earn.

I have a habit of thinking in moral terms about myself. If I’m not doing things the “right” way, I assume I am failing as a person, rather than simply living as a person. When I’m patient, I tell myself I’m good. When I’m impatient, I tell myself I’m wrong. When I’m productive, I tell myself I’m worthy. When I’m tired, I tell myself I’m less.

But worthiness isn’t a performance. It isn’t a salary. You don’t earn it by completing tasks. You don’t lose it because you slept late or because you didn’t call someone back quickly enough or because you had a day where you couldn’t make your best self show up.

Some people talk about self-worth as if it’s a switch you flip. Others talk about it as if it’s a philosophy. For me, it has always been something more practical: a decision I make in small increments. Like choosing to eat something nourishing instead of punishing myself with hunger. Like choosing to sit with discomfort without turning it into a verdict.

As I sat there, I thought about how easy it is to treat other people with the understanding you demand for yourself. You can forgive a friend’s flaws quickly, and yet you cannot forgive your own with the same generosity. It’s as if you believe that to be kind to yourself would be indulgent, and to be strict would be virtuous.

But strictness has its own kind of cruelty. It can be disciplined. It can be productive. It can also be corrosive. It can teach you to associate love with conditions.

I watched a couple on the path. They were arguing quietly, but their bodies carried the residue of earlier anger—shoulders tense, eyes narrowed. Then, unexpectedly, one of them smiled, and the tension softened. They walked for a few steps without speaking, simply together. Their reconciliation wasn’t dramatic, but it was real.

In that moment I saw a pattern: conflict doesn’t end a relationship unless it becomes the only language. People can repair. People can adjust. People can learn new rhythms.

That night, after dinner, I returned to my notebook. Not to add more tasks, not to punish myself for being behind. I wrote a single sentence: “Today happened.” It felt almost too simple, but simplicity has a way of disarming my need to interpret everything as a failure.

Then I wrote another sentence: “What did I notice?” I tried to remember the smallest things I’d brushed past earlier in the day. The woman with the paper bag. The smell of disinfectant. The laughter in the distance. The way the light on the bench shifted as clouds moved across the sky.

The next sentence I wrote was the one that surprised me: “I can practice noticing tomorrow, even if everything else stays difficult.”

That’s the kind of hope I can tolerate—not the fantasy hope that everything will work out, but the workable hope that I can change my relationship to what is.

Because life is not only made of major events. It is made of micro-moments, the small decisions that determine whether you move toward yourself or away from yourself. Whether you respond with honesty or with fear. Whether you treat the world as an enemy or as a place you have to negotiate.

Even the bus ride—those ordinary minutes—had been teaching me something about time. The bus schedule was indifferent to my readiness. The bus didn’t care if I felt prepared. It arrived anyway, carrying strangers with their own private weight.

And I realized: that is also how days are. They arrive. They carry people. They demand nothing about how you “feel” in order to continue moving forward. They are not a moral judgment. They are just movement.

When you accept that, you can stop trying to control the uncontrollable. You can still plan and still work and still make choices. But you stop treating every delay as proof that you are not enough. You stop treating every unfinished thing as evidence that you’ve already failed.

Later, after I had turned out the lights, I thought about the unfinished argument from years ago. It had kept returning like a draft. I wondered whether it would ever stop.

People say time heals everything, but I think time doesn’t heal so much as time gives you opportunities to look at your past from new angles. You begin to understand what you didn’t understand then. You begin to see the fear that drove your decisions. You begin to recognize the ways you were trying to protect something tender, without knowing how to protect it well.

It occurs to me that one of the most painful aspects of growing up is that you must live through the consequences of the earlier versions of yourself. You don’t get to redo the past. You only get to decide how to carry it.

I imagined calling the person from that argument. I didn’t know if the conversation would go well. I didn’t know if I’d have the right words. I didn’t even know if they would want to talk. But I felt, for the first time, that the question itself might not be punishment. It might be repair.

Repair is slow. It is not cinematic. It is often awkward. It requires you to be willing to look foolish and still continue. It requires you to accept that you cannot control the other person’s response.

In that sense, repair is similar to noticing. You do what you can with what you have. You try again.

The next morning, the quiet cruelty returned.

The air was thin. The sidewalk looked unfinished. The streetlights still lingered, as if the night had refused to exit. I walked toward the bus stop with the same body but a slightly different mind. I checked the clock. I didn’t take out my phone right away. I waited, and instead of treating waiting as a trap, I treated it as a pause.

The bus arrived with its sigh of brakes. I climbed aboard. I sat facing forward again, because sometimes old habits are the safest handholds. I listened to the small sounds inside the bus: the scrape of shoes, the soft rustle of clothing, the faint hum of the engine.

And I practiced noticing the people instead of treating them as obstacles. A man stared out the window with a faraway expression, as if he were navigating a memory. A teenager leaned their head back and closed their eyes, breathing as if they needed to reset. A child held a stuffed animal carefully, their thumb rubbing its fur in a repetitive comfort.

None of them were my responsibility, but all of them were evidence of something: life continuing in other bodies even when mine felt uncertain.

When we reached my stop, I stepped down and felt the cool air like a reminder that the world is real and present. I walked to where my day would take me, with its lists and appointments and interruptions.

I didn’t expect the day to become easy. I didn’t make myself a promise that I would become perfect.

Instead I made myself a smaller promise—one that felt like an actual tool.

I promised to return to the present when my mind tried to trap me in stories about failure. I promised to treat my feelings as information rather than verdicts. I promised to look for small repairs: a kind word, a thoughtful pause, a moment of honesty.

I promised to notice.

Because noticing is not passive. Noticing is a kind of courage. It is the act of refusing to be anesthetized by habit. It is choosing to see the world as it is, not as you fear it might become.

And if there is a quiet cruelty in morning, there is also a quiet mercy: the chance to begin again. Even if you begin late. Even if you begin imperfectly. Even if you begin with an unfinished argument still tugging at you like a loose thread.

The day will arrive whether you’re ready or not. The question is what you will do while it’s here—whether you will meet it with fear or with attention.

I met it with attention.

Not perfectly. Not heroically. Not in a way that would impress anyone who expects transformation to look like spectacle.

But enough to make the morning feel, if not kind, then at least honest.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I don’t actually have to write a particular kind of essay to satisfy a prompt like this, but I also don’t want to waste your time with empty filler. So I’ll write something that tries to be *worth reading*—not just “a lot of words,” but a coherent piece that moves.

---

At the edge of ordinary time, there are moments that feel like they were invented for stories: a stranger says the right sentence at the wrong moment, a train arrives early, a phone call comes from a number you don’t recognize, and it somehow still sounds like someone you love. People talk about fate in these situations, but fate is an easy word for a complicated feeling. The truth is that the world is always tilting—toward coincidence, toward meaning, toward loss—just not always in ways we can notice.

I used to think that life was made of events: birthdays, promotions, arguments, breakups, surgeries, deaths. Then I started noticing the quieter seams, the days that don’t appear on paper. The day I learned to make coffee the way someone else liked it, not because I wanted to impress them but because I paid attention. The day I swallowed my anger because the timing was wrong. The day I let myself sit in a room with nothing to do and realized that, without the constant friction of busyness, thoughts had their own weather system.

If you zoom out far enough, you can see how a person becomes a person. It’s not a dramatic transformation; it’s more like compost turning. Something put in the center at one moment—an insult, a compliment, a lesson overheard, a song heard in a car that wasn’t yours—rots and darkens and becomes useful months or years later. You don’t know what it will become. You only know that it changes your texture.

I didn’t grow up with the kind of home where feelings were discussed like facts, but I grew up with a home where they were *observed*. My family had the talent for measuring emotions without naming them. A chair scraped the floor differently when someone was upset. Silence lasted longer in certain rooms. The temperature of a conversation could shift even when the words remained steady. I learned early that people communicate not just with vocabulary but with timing, with posture, with the speed at which a hand moves.

That’s why, even now, when I look back at the past, I can’t help but see invisible signals running under everything. We weren’t speaking less—we were speaking in another dimension. The language of “fine,” for example. How often “fine” means “don’t ask,” and how often it means “I’m trying to survive the question that’s already in your eyes.” Or “no worries,” which might mean “I’m carrying something heavy and I don’t want to make you responsible for it.” Or the way someone says your name, not as an introduction but as an anchor, pulling you gently toward the present.

In my early adulthood, I chased the wrong kind of certainty. I thought clarity would arrive like a train—on schedule, announced, undeniable. I thought if I just made enough careful choices, I could engineer a life without surprises. But life is less like engineering and more like gardening. You plant, you water, you protect from frost, but there are still insects. There are storms. There are seasons you didn’t schedule.

I learned that certainty can be its own trap.

There was a time when I was sure I had to choose a single path and commit to it, as if the act of choosing locked my heart into one direction forever. I told myself that if I picked what felt safe, everything afterward would make sense. But “safe” is not the same as “true.” You can live in safety and still be stranded. You can be successful and still be lonely. You can be praised and still feel like you’re acting.

And then, as if the world grew tired of my denial, something small happened—small enough that if I tried to explain it, you might say it wasn’t worth the attention. I was walking somewhere I walked often, a route I could do with my eyes half closed. I noticed a patch of sunlight on the sidewalk that didn’t belong there, a warm rectangle among the gray. I stopped without thinking and stood in it, like a person who has just remembered their own body.

In that moment I felt—what? Relief? Gratitude? The word doesn’t matter. What mattered was that the feeling didn’t come from outside. It wasn’t induced by a phone notification or a conversation or a reward. It simply rose in me the way a scent rises when you open a drawer.

I didn’t tell anyone about it. I didn’t even name it. But later, when I was confronted with the old question—what do you do with your life?—that sunlight returned. It was a kind of calibration. It reminded me that a person is not only made from big decisions but from repeated moments of honesty with the self.

That’s when I started paying attention to what I wanted in a deeper way. Not what I wanted in the way you want a specific meal, craving satisfaction. But what I wanted in the way a compass wants north. What did I feel pulled toward, even when it wasn’t practical?

It turned out that what I wanted most was not a particular achievement. It was an atmosphere. I wanted a life with room in it. I wanted to be near people who did not require me to shrink. I wanted work that was not simply a transaction but a form of conversation. I wanted to create something, even if it was small, that made the world slightly more navigable.

This is one of those ideas that sounds poetic until you try to live it. Space is expensive. Time is expensive. The world tries to bill you for attention and then charges interest. There are bills you can’t avoid—healthcare, rent, obligations. There is also the less visible cost: the cost of being unfaithful to yourself. Every time you choose what doesn’t fit, you pay. The payment isn’t always immediate, but it accrues.

I began to notice the payments I’d already made without knowing. I’d spent months—years, actually—doing work that looked impressive but drained me. I’d spent time with people who were generous in conversation but stingy in care. I’d made decisions that satisfied other people’s expectations while quieting my own instincts. I’d treated my intuition like something childish, something to be corrected.

The correction never came. Instead, my life became a room with furniture arranged for someone else. Functional, perhaps. But you don’t inhabit it. You pass through it.

So I tried a different approach: not “change everything,” but “change the questions.”

Instead of “Is this the right path?” I asked, “Does this path make me more myself or less?” Instead of “Am I failing?” I asked, “What am I avoiding?” Instead of “What will impress people?” I asked, “What would satisfy my conscience?” It’s surprising how quickly your life shifts when the metrics change.

Of course, there’s still fear. There’s always fear. Even when you know better, fear keeps an office in your mind. It manages your worst-case scenarios. It tells you that the familiar route is safer than the unknown one, even when the familiar route is already hurting you.

Fear has a way of sounding like wisdom. It says: Wait. Don’t risk it. Hold off. Be careful. In moderation, fear can protect you. In excess, it paralyzes you. The challenge is to recognize fear as a voice among voices, not the whole chorus.

It’s also hard to explain to other people what you’re doing when you start changing. Some people will accuse you of drama or lack of discipline. Some will be genuinely concerned. They may not understand that your life isn’t a test they’re grading. It’s a process you’re trying to survive with as much integrity as possible.

Sometimes the people you disappoint will be the people who cared about you most. That’s a particular pain. You want to be loyal, but loyalty shouldn’t require self-erasure. Love that depends on your quiet compliance is not love; it’s control in a softer costume.

I learned to measure relationships by another metric: reciprocity. Not exactly tit-for-tat, not keeping score like a bitter accountant, but a sense of mutual effort. When one person is always reaching and the other is always waiting, that imbalance becomes a kind of slow drought. You start to shrink your needs because you don’t want to feel like a burden. Then you forget what your needs even were.

I’ve been on both sides of that drought.

It’s easy to romanticize the idea of “the one who understands.” But understanding is not magic. It’s a practice. People who understand you do so because they keep showing up—with attention, with patience, with the willingness to be wrong. They listen as if your interior life is real. They don’t use your vulnerability as a way to win arguments.

And when understanding fails—as it always does—there’s another practice: repair. The ability to come back after a misstep, to apologize without burying the apology under excuses. The ability to say, “I see how that hurt,” even if it wasn’t your intention. Intentions are important, but impact is the truth you can’t negotiate.

Repair is how you build a life that can withstand the inevitable. Not a life without conflict. A life that can handle conflict without collapsing.

I used to think stability meant avoiding storms. Now I think stability means being able to rebuild after storms.

There are days I still struggle with that. I can be harsh with myself, suspicious of happiness. I can feel like I don’t deserve the quiet good things unless I’m earning them with some kind of suffering. It’s a habit from somewhere—maybe a cultural habit, maybe a family habit, maybe just the human habit of interpreting discomfort as a signal that something is wrong.

But there is a difference between healthy discomfort and pointless misery. Growth can hurt. But not every hurt is growth. Sometimes hurt is simply the body’s record of choices you regret or circumstances you cannot control.

I began to treat my own well-being with the seriousness I once reserved for other people’s approval. That shift changed everything about how I move through the day. I stopped asking, “What can I do to be acceptable?” and started asking, “What do I need to be okay?” Those questions don’t always lead to perfect answers. Sometimes the answer is boring: sleep. Sometimes it’s difficult: boundaries. Sometimes it’s both: sleep, and boundaries, and then sleep again.

And sometimes the answer is: do something small that matches your values. It’s easy to get overwhelmed by the scale of your life and believe you need a grand transformation to matter. But values don’t require grand gestures. They require consistency.

Values are like threads. You weave them. You keep going even when the pattern isn’t finished. When you stop weaving—when you betray your own priorities for the sake of convenience—you notice the fabric thinning. It’s subtle at first. You can still walk around wearing the garment, but it doesn’t fit your life anymore. You become uncomfortable in your own skin, and you blame yourself for it, as if you’re the problem rather than the misalignment.

I learned to stop blaming myself for misalignment.

Misalignment is data. It tells you something doesn’t fit. It tells you what you can adjust. When you notice misalignment, you don’t need to spiral into self-hatred. You can simply plan.

That planning looks different for everyone. I’m not going to pretend there’s a universal formula. Some people make decisions by leaving abruptly. Some people make decisions by staying long enough to secure a bridge. Some people need therapy; some need a friend who doesn’t flinch when they say the difficult thing. Some people need money; some need community; some need time. Many need a combination.

But the most important thing is to recognize when you’re stuck in a story rather than living a life.

The story I once lived was: if I’m patient and careful and hardworking, I will eventually be rewarded with relief. In that story, relief was the final prize after a long race. But what if relief isn’t the prize? What if relief is the evidence that you’re moving in the right direction? What if the goal isn’t to earn safety but to live in it as much as possible?

The problem with waiting is that waiting can become a form of self-abandonment. You keep telling yourself that you’ll start later, after the next deadline, after the next promotion, after the next relationship stabilizes, after the next tragedy, after the next wave of anxiety passes.

Meanwhile your life keeps happening. You can’t postpone your existence indefinitely.

So I tried to live in the present with more courage. Not with reckless optimism, but with a kind of disciplined tenderness. I let myself enjoy what was good without immediately questioning whether it was deserved. I let myself be impressed by beauty and not treat it as a distraction. I let myself be a beginner at things that terrified me because I wanted mastery, not just competence. I allowed myself to be ordinary on days when I didn’t have energy to be exceptional.

One of the strangest gifts of paying attention is that you begin to notice what you used to ignore. The world is filled with subtle choreography: a neighbor’s plants reaching for light; the way people in a subway car adjust their shoulders when someone new enters; the way silence becomes different after you’ve said something honest. You start to see that life is not only composed of moments of drama. It’s composed of thousands of micro-decisions made by people who have no idea you’re watching.

That awareness makes me gentler. It also makes me more demanding about how I treat others. Because if you really believe everyone is making micro-decisions, you stop assuming that their actions are about you. You stop turning everything into a referendum on your worth.

You begin to ask: what is this person carrying? What do they know? What do they fear? What do they need? You still set boundaries, because compassion isn’t the same as tolerance for harm. But you choose your response with more information and less ego.

There’s another reason I pay attention now: I’m haunted by the idea that I could miss the best part. Not the grand moments, but the quiet ones. The best part of life might not be a wedding or a promotion or a famous recognition. It might be the part that happens when nobody’s watching. The part where you decide to forgive. The part where you apologize quickly. The part where you stay kind when you could be cruel and instead choose to be accurate. The part where you let yourself rest without earning it through suffering.

I think people underestimate how radical rest can be.

Rest isn’t laziness. Rest is maintenance. It’s what keeps you from becoming a machine that runs until it breaks. When you rest, you restore attention. You restore curiosity. You restore empathy. You stop living as if everything is urgent.

Urgency is one of the world’s favorite illusions. It wants your nervous system because a nervous system is easy to manipulate. It can sell you solutions to problems you never had, it can convince you that you’re behind, that you should be anxious for the sake of productivity.

Rest is resistance.

Rest is choosing not to be driven like an object. It’s choosing to steer your own time. It’s choosing to trust that you can care for your future without sacrificing your present.

This doesn’t mean I’m always successful at it. I have seasons where I do better and seasons where I slip into old patterns. But I no longer treat slipping as proof that I’m doomed. I treat it as part of being human. The world is changeable, and so are we.

There’s an odd comfort in accepting change. It means the story is not fixed. It means you can revise your life without having to pretend the past didn’t happen. It means your current pain doesn’t automatically mean you’re stuck. It means the future is not only a continuation—it’s also a departure.

Departure is another word that sounds dramatic, but it can be small: a decision to stop answering certain messages; a decision to tell the truth in a kind way; a decision to begin again after you’ve lost your way; a decision to stop trying to earn love through performance.

I remember once meeting someone who seemed to have made peace with themselves. They weren’t perfect. They had their own anxieties. But their presence had a kind of steadiness. They didn’t rush to justify their existence. They didn’t apologize for taking up space. When they listened, it felt like they were making room.

After talking with them, I felt something loosen inside me. Not jealousy. Not imitation. Something like permission.

Permission to be unfinished. Permission to be afraid and still proceed. Permission to hope without bargaining. Permission to admit that I didn’t have it all figured out.

That is the thing about permission: it is contagious.

When you give yourself permission to be a real person—flawed, evolving, full of contradictions—you become more honest with other people. You stop demanding certainty and start seeking connection. You stop trying to win and start trying to understand. You stop treating life like an audition and start treating it like a relationship.

And relationships, all relationships, require effort. They require time. They require listening. They require repair. They require the humility to accept that you can’t control everything.

There is a particular kind of grief that comes from accepting limits. You want to hold on to people and situations and outcomes, but you can’t hold everything. You can’t keep every promise. You can’t prevent every loss. You can’t make the world safe enough to relax into it forever.

So what do you do?

You grieve, first. You let yourself feel. You let sadness be a signal rather than a verdict. Then, after you grieve, you do what humans have always done: you build. You build small routines that keep you afloat. You build friendships. You build creative projects. You build trust slowly. You build a sense of meaning that doesn’t depend on never being hurt.

Meaning is not a magic property of the world. It’s a practice. You decide what matters and you act accordingly. Sometimes you act well. Sometimes you act badly. But you keep returning to the question: what kind of person do I want to be?

That question is so powerful because it outlasts many specific circumstances. If your finances change, your values can remain. If your relationships shift, your values can still guide you. If you lose something, values can help you decide what to do with the remaining parts of your life.

I wish I could tell you that I figured this out once and for all. I didn’t. I learned it the way you learn weather patterns—through repetition, through seasons, through consequences. I learned it as I watched myself respond to different kinds of stress. I learned it as I made mistakes and then had to sit with what those mistakes meant. I learned it as I experienced moments of unexpected kindness that reminded me the world is more complex than my fear.

Sometimes, in the middle of a normal day, I feel the tilt again—the world leaning toward coincidence, toward meaning, toward something that feels almost like grace. Maybe it’s a song in the grocery store. Maybe it’s a child laughing. Maybe it’s the sudden realization that I’m not stuck in the past. Maybe it’s the quiet certainty that even if I’m not where I want to be, I’m still moving.

That movement matters. Not because it guarantees a happy ending, but because movement proves you’re alive in your own story.

The best stories are rarely about perfection. They’re about attention. They’re about courage. They’re about how people change when the world presses in. They’re about what remains when you peel away all the performances.

So when I think about writing freely, I think about attention. I think about the way words can become a kind of lantern—small, imperfect, but capable of showing you the next step. I think about how a life can be like that too: not a grand monument, but a series of steps you take while trying to see honestly.

If you’re reading this and you feel stuck, I want to say something simple: you don’t have to resolve everything to begin. Begin with noticing. Begin with one true question. Begin with one kind action toward yourself or toward someone else. Begin with rest, if you’ve forgotten how.

And if you’re not stuck—if you’re in a season that feels stable or even happy—then I hope you notice that too. Happiness is not something to hoard like contraband. It’s something to inhabit. Let it change you, like sunlight on a sidewalk. Let it remind you that you are capable of more than endurance.

The world will keep tilting. That’s what the world does. It tilts toward coincidence and meaning and loss, toward healing and misunderstanding and repair. Your job isn’t to control it.

Your job is to meet it with as much honesty as you can.

Because life, in the end, isn’t only made of events. It’s made of the moments between them—the pauses, the glances, the choices that don’t look like choices until you look back and see the thread.

And once you see the thread, you realize you weren’t just living randomly. You were learning how to live.
